title: Why School Is the Oldest and Most Effective Educational Technology
author: Didau, David
summary: David Didau builds an evolutionary argument for why schools are humanity's most powerful and culturally essential educational technology, grounding his case in gene-culture coevolution theory and the cognitive science of social vs. asocial learning. The central claim is that human brains are not just built for culture -- they are built by culture -- the result of 2.5 million years of gene-culture co-evolution in which social learning (copying what others have learned) dramatically outcompeted asocial learning (trial and error) in terms of survival efficiency. Schools exist as the formalised, optimised vessel for this social learning: they solve the problem of transmitting cultural knowledge quickly, efficiently, and equitably to each new generation, in a world where the pace of cultural change vastly exceeds biological evolution's speed. Didau traces this through Kevin Laland's evolutionary biology, distinguishing why human brains evolved to be social learning machines rather than independent discoverers, and why this has profound implications for pedagogy: the brain evolved for social, guided, efficient transmission of knowledge -- not for independent discovery or trial-and-error in educational contexts. The article is explicitly critical of educational fashions that assume children's brains are discovery-optimised rather than transmission-optimised, and treats the school as a cultural achievement that allows each generation to inherit rather than re-derive the intellectual capital of the past.
points: Human beings survive not through individual cleverness but through the accumulated cultural knowledge of previous generations -- the brain evolved specifically to absorb and build on what others have already figured out, making social learning the foundation of human success.

Schools are not arbitrary historical accidents but the formalised solution to a real evolutionary problem: how does each generation inherit complex cultural knowledge efficiently, given that individual trial-and-error learning is both costly and slow?

The 2.5-million-year gene-culture coevolution that produced the human brain produced a brain optimised for social transmission, not independent discovery -- a fact that has profound pedagogical implications for how classrooms should be organised.

Asocial learning (trial-and-error, discovery) is accurate but expensive -- you can get killed testing the mushroom, literally or metaphorically -- while social learning (copying, instruction) is efficient because it amortises the cost of one person's learning across many subsequent learners.

The ability to inherit culture -- and thereby judge it, use it, extend it, and when necessary resist it -- depends on first receiving it; originality is not the opposite of cultural transmission but one of its eventual products.
quotes: Unlike any other species, we have survived and thrived not because of strength or speed, but because of our ability to learn from one another. Cultural innovations have been passed down through generations via a process of social learning.

Our brains have evolved not to rediscover the world anew, but to benefit from what others have already figured out. Of course, this doesn't mean that the point of education is passive acceptance of whatever has been handed down.
In the words of evolutionary biologist Kevin Laland, 'Human minds are not just built for culture; they are built by culture.'
A school is not just buildings where children are kept busy; it is an example of humanity's most powerful tool for transmitting cultural knowledge quickly, efficiently, and equitably.

The advantage of asocial learning is that you get accurate, up-to-date, first-hand information about what works and what doesn't, but the cost is high. You could waste hours on strategies that barely work -- or worse, you might end up dead after eating a suspiciously funky mushroom.
Without schools, we risk forcing each child to start from scratch in a world that's far too complex, far too unforgiving, for such inefficiency.
